Fun game, but there are a few small things that could make it more realistic. One thing I noticed is when your character holds the gun, he doesn’t shake like in the Flash version. In that one, the hand holding the gun would visibly shake, which added tension. Also, your character doesn’t look around the room just stares forward. In the Flash game, both the player and opponent would look around, which made it feel way more alive. Right now, the opponent just stares, and even though they make some faces, it still feels stiff. Adding that head movement or looking around while waiting would make a huge difference. I know most people won’t wait around long in game, but I personally love attention to detail it really adds to the immersion. So in short: character arm shake when holding the gun, and head movement while deciding or waiting (for both your character and the opponent). Those things were in the Flash game and really helped. Sorry if my writing is bad, it’s around midnight and I’m tired, but I think you get what I mean The game is fun, I just think a few added details would make it even more awesome. Like maybe more expressions for newer characters, and in Story Mode, the character order should be random each time instead of being the same every playthrough. I don’t know why it’s always the same but yeah. Also two-player Orange Royale would be amazing so me and my family can play together. A small thing I noticed: when the orange dude with glasses dies, his glasses just vanish. If that’s intentional, maybe show an animation of them falling off or sticking to the body. And sometimes some of the fingers on certain characters bend in weird ways, so that could use a quick fix. One gameplay thing too: I usually die the second I get the gun. It feels like the bullet is always in chamber one, so when I click myself, I just die right away. I’m not sure if it’s truly random between 1/6 and 6/6, but it feels like the bullet is either in the first or last chamber like 50% of the time. But aside from that, I really love the hats and accessories, and the part where that crazy dude tricks you into giving you the gun but pulls back about three times that was such a cool detail. I also wish where sometimes when you or the your opponent get the gun they either just grab it fast or take a while, would be a good detail, I don't know why and it would be cool if the opponent maybe sometimes took longer or something to decide his choice.

So, I never grew up with orange roulette. I recently discovered this game and its flash version not too long ago, and I can see why this game stuck with so many people. Really tense and fun game if you have some time to spare, and I really like how each orange you go up against have their own details that add a lot of character to them, like how the sad orange crosses his fingers whenever he or you are about to shoot the banana gun. Def a surprisingly peak game that deserves more attention.

Orange Roulette takes an absurd concept and transforms it into a surprisingly engaging psychological survival game that thrives on tension, uncertainty, and dark humor. Developed by Mikey Houser and published by Loserville Express, the game throws players into an eccentric world where imprisoned oranges are forced to participate in a deadly contest orchestrated by ruthless apples. Their only chance of earning freedom is to survive a dangerous game centered around the mysterious Banana Gun, whose randomly ripening seed functions as the game's unpredictable source of danger. While the premise initially feels like a comedy built around food-themed characters, it quickly reveals a much darker atmosphere that makes every decision feel meaningful. At its heart, the gameplay revolves around balancing probability with instinct. Every round asks players to evaluate risk, determine whether to trust chance, and make difficult choices under pressure. Rather than relying on fast-paced combat or complex mechanics, Orange Roulette succeeds by creating suspense through uncertainty. The Banana Gun's random nature ensures that every encounter carries genuine tension, making victories feel rewarding because they result from a combination of careful thinking and good fortune. This straightforward but effective design keeps players invested, as no situation ever feels entirely predictable and each session unfolds differently depending on the decisions made. The presentation plays a major role in establishing the game's identity. Bright colors, expressive fruit characters, and exaggerated animations create the impression of a cheerful cartoon, but that lighthearted appearance contrasts sharply with the grim circumstances unfolding beneath the surface. This clash between playful visuals and unsettling subject matter gives the experience a memorable personality. Environmental details, expressive character designs, and well-timed sound effects all contribute to an atmosphere that shifts seamlessly between humor and anxiety. Moments of silence are just as impactful as dramatic audio cues, reinforcing the sense that danger is never far away despite the whimsical aesthetic. Although the story remains intentionally strange, it provides enough context to make the bizarre setting compelling. The imprisoned oranges are more than simple comedic characters, as their struggle for survival adds emotional weight to the game's unusual premise. Instead of delivering lengthy exposition, the narrative unfolds naturally through gameplay and environmental storytelling, allowing players to piece together the harsh reality of this fruit-filled prison. Multiple endings encourage experimentation by rewarding different decisions and outcomes, giving players additional reasons to revisit the game and discover alternative conclusions while uncovering more of its peculiar world. Replayability is one of Orange Roulette's strongest qualities. Randomized scenarios prevent encounters from becoming repetitive, while unlockable achievements and branching endings provide meaningful incentives to continue playing beyond a single completion. Because luck alone cannot guarantee success, players gradually develop a better understanding of the game's strategic elements with every attempt. The focused scope also works in its favor, delivering an experience that remains consistently engaging without unnecessary filler or prolonged pacing. Its modest hardware requirements further make it accessible to a broad audience looking for an inventive indie title. Orange Roulette succeeds because it embraces originality instead of chasing familiar trends. Its unusual setting, clever blend of strategy and psychological suspense, and memorable visual style create an experience that stands apart from conventional survival games. Beneath its humorous exterior lies a surprisingly effective examination of fear, chance, and perseverance, proving that even the strangest concepts can become compelling when supported by thoughtful design. Players seeking a distinctive indie experience filled with tension, replay value, and offbeat charm will likely find plenty to appreciate in this unconventional adventure. Rating: 8/10
